⁠

⁠

In some parts of the world, aging means doing the impossible.⁠
⁠
Imagine being 80 years-old free diving 65 feet underwater (with no oxygen tank) to harvest abalone, conch, seaweed, sea urchin and octopus. ⁠
⁠
Holding their breath for up to two minutes, these are the Haenyeo women of Jeju Island. They’re part of a 400-year-old tradition born from survival and necessity, where many began diving as young as 11.⁠
⁠
But this living legacy is slowly disappearing as younger generations are choosing universities and safer careers. ⁠
⁠
Today, we learn from these keepers of tradition and the incredible strength and endurance it takes to do this every day. 💙⁠

caption:
Same foods. Very different food systems.

In the U.S., thousands of additives are allowed in our food supply, and many of them are banned or restricted in Europe. 

A lot of them never went through independent FDA review. Under a loophole called GRAS (“generally recognized as safe”), companies can decide for themselves that an ingredient is safe and put it on the market.

A few examples:

🍊 U.S. Fanta: high fructose corn syrup, Red 40, Yellow 6. Europe: carrot and pumpkin extract.
🍞 Potassium bromate, a dough conditioner banned in the EU, UK, and Canada, is still allowed in U.S. bread.
🐔 U.S. chicken can be rinsed in chlorine. The EU doesn’t allow it.
🍟 U.S. fast food fries can list a dozen or more ingredients. Elsewhere, it’s often potatoes, oil, and salt.

None of this is an accident. 

Our food system rewards cheap, shelf-stable, hyperpalatable products, and our farm policy subsidizes the corn and soy behind them. That’s the system I wrote about in Food Fix.

Europe isn’t perfect. But it shows what happens when precaution comes first.

Until our policies change, read labels and eat as close to whole, real food as you can.

Note - These images are digitally rendered for illustration. They reflect real differences in ingredients and food standards between the U.S. and Europe. Credit: @mental.maxing

caption:
New data just dropped: only 54% of Americans drink alcohol now - the LOWEST rate in 90 years.

That’s a 13-point crash in just 3 years. Something massive is happening, and if you’ve been questioning your relationship with alcohol, you’re part of a historic health revolution.

Here’s what’s driving this seismic shift:
- Young adults are leading with remarkable clarity - only 50% drink now (down from 72% in 2004).
- Women are stepping back in record numbers - down 11 points in just one year.
- Even drinkers are drinking dramatically less - only 24% had alcohol yesterday (record low), and the average is just 2.8 drinks per week.

As a doctor, I’ll say it clearly: No amount of alcohol is safe for human health. The idea that moderate drinking has benefits was based on flawed research. We now know alcohol causes 100,000+ cancer cases yearly and 20,000 preventable deaths.

Your liver processes alcohol as a toxin because that’s exactly what it is.

If you do choose to drink occasionally, see my other post on minimizing damage. But know this: 53% of Americans now understand that even “moderate” drinking is harmful - nearly double from 2015.

Ultra-processed foods now make up almost half of the average Australian diet.

And the research is clear: the more you rely on them, the higher your risk for chronic disease.

But not all UPFs look like junk food, and not all of them are automatically “bad.”

The real issue may be that many are loaded with salt, sugar, saturated fats and energy density that push our bodies into long-term trouble.

We try to be realistic when working with Everlab members on optimising their health. And it's simply not realistic for most people to cut these foods out of their life completely.

Our dietitians recommends aiming to reduce to 80/20.

Build your plate around whole foods most of the time, and use UPFs for convenience. 

After all, leaning into convenience here and there can reduce stress, which is also a key part of reducing disease risk.

Picture yourself at 75.

Are you sharp and strong or struggling with focus and mobility?

Super-agers are people in their 70s, 80s, or even 90s whose memory and thinking skills match those decades younger.

Super-agers don’t just stay sharp mentally — they’re also more likely to remain physically healthy and independent as they age.

Science shows their brains actually LOOK different. A super-ager’s memory regions shrink more slowly, helping them resist decline.

Genetics play a role, lifestyle choices are powerful.

Regular physical activity, learning new skills, strong social connections, quality sleep, and a balanced diet are all habits linked to super-agers.

The best time to start protecting your brain and body is always right now.

Start tracking your health early and make changes that set you up for long-term vitality.

caption:
It’s not science fiction. As mitochondria convert nutrients into energy (ATP), they release tiny bursts of light called ultraweak photon emissions (UPE), too faint to see with the naked eye.⁠
⁠
But scientists are discovering this light may be more than just a byproduct of cellular activity.⁠
⁠
In a 2023 study, researchers stressed one group of isolated mitochondria while keeping another group unstressed. Even though the two groups couldn’t touch or exchange chemicals, the unstressed mitochondria still changed their behavior — suggesting mitochondria may communicate through light-based signals.⁠
⁠
TLDR: Mitochondria aren’t just powerhouses of the cell, they’re shaping up to be dynamic communicators, constantly sensing and responding to their environment. ⁠
⁠
Source: Mould, Rhys R., et al. “Non-chemical Signalling Between Mitochondria.” Frontiers in Physiology, September 22, 2023, Volume 14, Article 1268075. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2023.1268075/full ⁠

caption:
Did you know this? ⬆️

The field of sociogenomics reveals how positive relationships influence gene expression, turning on genes that repair cells and turning off genes associated with inflammation and disease.

When you experience love and connection, your body releases hormones like oxytocin and endorphins, which calm the nervous system, lower cortisol levels (the stress hormone), and promote anti-inflammatory pathways. 

These hormonal shifts signal your genes to activate cellular repair and longevity mechanisms. Even physical touch, like cuddling, can boost oxytocin and enhance your immune system.

On the flip side, chronic stress, isolation, or conflict triggers the expression of pro-inflammatory genes, accelerating aging and increasing your risk of chronic illness.

Love and connection are powerful for health and longevity.

caption:
GRIP STRENGTH & LONGEVITY: “LIVE HANGS” 

Congratulations Ann Crile Esselstyn, who at *90 years and 231 days* old (title card says 93), did a continual bar grip hang for 2 minutes and 52 seconds. (And set a @guinnessworldrecords WR)

Grip strength and grip endurance (not exactly the same thing) are correlates of longevity. They are great to train for but grip strength alone does not extend life. So what do they reflect?

We often think about the muscle aspect of grip. To me,the really interesting data = the relationship between grip and longevity of *cognitive functioning*.

Why would there be a relationship there?

In neuroscience, we refer to the upper and the lower motor neurons. Upper motor neurons are in the brain and are involved in deliberate action (among other things); lower motor neurons are in the spinal cord and directly connect to the muscles by extending out of the central nervous system into the peripheral nervous system. They directly cause muscles to contract.

We also think about proximal muscles, which are the muscle muscles near the midline and distal muscles like those tips of your calves, forearms, fingers and toes.

Early but compelling evidence suggest that distal strength— the motor neuron control of the parts of your body furthest from your midline, is one of the first things to atrophy as you age. 

You can offset this with strong, gripping, keeping your feet, strong, calves, etc.

So while it’s important to train your core and the muscles of your legs, chest back and arms, don’t forget about feet yes feet! 

And hands and forearms. It’s not just about aesthetics. It’s very likely about maintaining those upper motor brain neurons. 

Once specific sets of neurons in the brain start to die off they often take others with them, the so-called bystander effect.

More on this in a Huberman Lab podcast to come but meanwhile, wherever you’re at in your fitness in longevity training the whole body and keep going! And congrats to Ann. That’s a super impressive timing at any age! 

Please put any questions you have below and thank you for your interest in science!

STIMULATE MUSCLE GROWTH PROPERLY: 
BACK DAY WITH @thedorianyates (6 time Mr. Olympia) •

Comment BACK & I’ll DM you a link to a video of the full workout @goldsgym.venice 

There are a lot of studies and examples of different ways to train with weights for muscle growth and strength. Which is best? 

Everyone has different opinions on that but what works best for me has been low volume high intensity training. (And when I say “best”, I mean getting the results of directed muscle growth and strength improvements and not having my nervous system feel so fried that I can’t do other things after training… after all, we have lives to live!)

It involves training 3 days per week & each muscle directly 1X per week. Yes only once. You do 1 light set & 1 moderate set just to get the mechanics and blood flow going, then 1 (maybe 2) all out sets to failure *in excellent form* which means controlling the weight all the way up, contracting it hard and lowering it slowly. Depending on the muscle group, you do anywhere from 2 to 4 exercises per muscle group total. 

6 time Mr. Olympia @thedorianyates is my guest on the Huberman Lab podcast out now and we discussed this style of training and the types of training that work best for the everyday person. That means men & women of all ages. He gives a wealth of info.

Dorian was also kind enough to take me through his version of low volume high intensity training. I got to feel what it is to target the back and rear delt muscles properly with true high intensity.

We did:

1) lat pullovers: one light set, one medium set, and then one all outset to failure (w/ a few assisted repetitions).

2) reverse grip cable pull downs (also one set to failure)

3) one arm dumbbell rows (one set to failure for each side)

4) seated wide grip cable rows (one set to failure with a couple of assisted reps)

5) rear delt bent over dumbbell raises (one warm-up and one works set to failure).

MUCH OF LEARNING (IN DOGS & HUMANS) IS TOP DOWN INHIBITION •

Much of learning involves adjusting the connections between the prefrontal cortex and deeper brain structures that control impulses. Indeed, if you look at motor learning in humans or other mammals, you’ll notice that most of building a skill is about eliminating incorrect aspects of a movement.

This is my second bulldog mutt, and as with the last one (Costello) I started the training early at 9 weeks. 

Strummer is doing a great job learning to suppress his impulse to move aka “sit” and to come when called, to stay calm around food and all the rest. 

Dogs have a tiny prefrontal cortex relative to humans but they can multipurpose it to learn lots of things and lots of different scenarios. They are oh so smart. But it is kind of fun to think about how they’re training you as well.

Indeed training a bulldog breed (because they’re so stubborn) is also about training yourself in patience. Strummer is part mastiff and boxer/pit too but he’s still been giving us a run for our money on the patience side! What he doesn’t know is I’ve done this before. And it’s been pure pleasure.

NOTE: I want to be thoughtful in sharing any post about a bulldog and how great they are because they have wonderful personalities, but they are not trivial to raise properly and take care of properly so if you decide to take that on understand it will take many hours per day or more to train them up and to keep them healthy. If they’re just allowed to sleep and you let them just kind of move around like sea turtles they get very unhealthy and unhappy. 

I suggest getting a mutt because they tend to be a little bit easier, but then they’ll also have more energy. So then you’ve got a stubborn high energy dog! But they have huge hearts, like no other breed (in my opinion). 

We can learn a lot from dogs. And other animals and our interactions w/them -not just observing them.

caption:
Can ADHD symptoms be reduced through diet? A randomized controlled trial suggests that, for some children, the answer may be yes.

Published in The Lancet, the study included 100 children with ADHD. Half followed a closely supervised, five-week elimination diet that removed many commonly eaten foods, including artificial additives, gluten, dairy, added sugar, and other potential triggers.

The results were striking:

🔬 Among the children who completed the elimination diet, 78% experienced a significant reduction in ADHD symptoms.

🔄 When foods were reintroduced in a blinded challenge, symptoms returned in 63% of responders—suggesting that certain foods may influence symptoms in a subset of children.

ADHD is complex, and food is not the only factor. But diet can affect blood sugar, nutrient status, the gut microbiome, inflammation, and the production of neurotransmitters involved in attention, mood, and behavior.

So what’s the next step?

If your child struggles with ADHD, consider working with a qualified clinician to explore whether food may be contributing:

1. Temporarily remove artificial additives, ultra-processed foods, added sugar, gluten, dairy, and other suspected triggers under professional supervision.
2. Focus on whole, nutrient-dense foods, including high-quality protein, healthy fats, fiber, and phytonutrient-rich vegetables.
3. Support gut health with fiber-rich and fermented foods when tolerated.
4. Balance blood sugar with protein, fiber, and healthy fats at every meal.

Medication can have an important place in ADHD treatment, but it may not be the only tool available. We should also be asking: What factors could be amplifying these symptoms?

For some children, a carefully supervised elimination diet may be one missing piece of the puzzle.

DOI: 10.1016/S0140-6736(10)62227-1

Your brain evolved for movement.
It solves problems best not in stillness, but in motion.

Start walking. It’s one of the most powerful forms of medicine we have.

Cesar Milan aka the Dog Whisperer was my guest on the recent Huberman Lab podcast. 

Most people do not walk their dogs enough and it causes their dogs to be anxious and unhealthy much of the time. 
Most dogs need at least 30 min brisk walks (and up to 60 min or more) twice per day every day. Some breeds need far more. 

Tiring out your dog is so crucial to their wellbeing. The daily walks are of course also good for you. People often ask me if the morning sunlight viewing I always talk about for humans pertains to animals too and the short answer is yes: absolutely — same neurons in the eyes and brain govern the improved mood and sleep that morning sun viewing triggers.

I raised both my bulldog-mastiffs (and pit) mutts using Cesar’s methods and they worked terrifically well both times… and that is a stubborn (and in the case of Strummer, my second dog also super energetic) breed.

The 2, 45-60 min structured walks per day were/are what  is needed and often a good 4mike hike on the weekend and mid week too. 

People debate dog training methods but to my knowledge, everyone agrees that dogs need exercise. Also, the vets I consulted (I have one in my family!) confirmed most people just don’t exercise their dogs nearly enough.

caption:
Lab-grown meat just cleared another hurdle.

Cultivated salmon, chicken, and pork fat have now cleared FDA and USDA review, and they are already showing up on menus and in products around the country.

Here is what concerns me. Most of what gets marketed as “cultivated meat” is not a whole cut of meat grown in a lab. It is a hybrid: cultivated animal cells blended with plant proteins, refined oils, starches, and flavorings to imitate the taste and texture of the real thing. That is a heavily formulated food, not a whole one.

These products are being sold as a more sustainable, ethical alternative to conventional meat. Maybe someday the data will back that up. Right now we do not have long-term safety research or proof that they deliver on the environmental promises at scale.

I would rather eat real food with a known nutritional profile than a lab-formulated product we are still learning about. My recommendation has not changed: choose organic, pasture-raised, grass-fed meat and wild-caught fish whenever you can. These foods come from animals raised the way nature intended, without a list of processing ingredients required to make them taste like food.

Swipe through to see what is actually in these products and what to look for on the label.

Plastic blenders are a source of microplastics that most people overlook.

Those with plastic jars or pitchers release microplastics, and even nanoplastics, into blended food or drinks due to friction and mechanical abrasion during blending.

A single 30-second blending cycle can release up to 1 billion (yes, with a “b”) micro- and nanoplastic particles.

BPA-free products are safer but can still release particles due to heavy use, heat, or abrasion. My advice is to switch to a completely stainless-steel blender. It’s the only way to avoid contamination.

Thanks to @steven for allowing me to audit his kitchen! Check out the full episode.

caption:
Syrniki reinvented😜
One of my favourite Slavic desserts is Syrniki. It is made with curd cheese. They usually give them a round, slightly flattened shape and fry them in the pan one by one, but I decided to give Syrniki a European touch and baked them in cupcake cases in the oven. Less hassle, more enjoyment😉 

The recipe is very easy. The only thing is the curd cheese itself which you can buy only in Slavic shops in London. Brits don't usually have it.
I bought 2 packs (250gr each) of Polish curd cheese, they call it twarog, which is the same in other Slavic languages. 1 egg, 3-4 tb. spoons of erythritol (I don't use sugar any more to keep my blood sugar levels normal), 3 tb. spoons of oat flour, and a dash of vanilla syrup. Mix it with a blender, and that's it!
Then you just put the mixture into the cupcake cases and bake in the oven(180° for 25 mins). Take them out and let to cool down. Turn them over and serve with any topping. My fav is soured cream. This recipe makes 12 syrniks. Enjoy! 😁😋😊✨️✨️
Переосмысление сырников😜
Один из моих любимых славянских десертов — сырники. Он готовится из творога. Обычно им придают круглую, слегка приплюснутую форму и обжаривают на сковороде по одному, но я решила придать сырникам европейский колорит и запекла их в формочках для кексов в духовке. Меньше хлопот, больше удовольствия😉 

Рецепт очень простой. Единственное, что нужно — это сам творог, который можно купить только в славянских магазинах в Лондоне. У британцев его обычно нет.
Я купила 2 пачки (по 250 г) польского творога, его называют twarog, что то же самое и в других славянских языках. 1 яйцо, 3-4 ст. ложки эритритола (я больше не использую сахар, чтобы поддерживать нормальный уровень сахара в крови), 3 ст. ложки овсяной муки и немного ванильного сиропа. Смешиваю блендером, и все!
 Затем просто положите смесь в формочки для кексов и выпекайте в духовке (180° в течение 25 минут). Достаньте их и дайте остыть. Переверните и подавайте с любой начинкой. Мой любимый вариант — сметана. По этому рецепту получается 12 сырников. Наслаждайтесь! 😁😋😊✨️✨️

caption:
It’s okay to add a banana to your blueberry smoothie. Bananas are nutritious, I eat them, and this is not a reason to stop. But if your goal is to preserve as many of the berry polyphenols as possible, the chemistry matters. 
 
A small, acute study in eight healthy men compared standardized cocoa flavan-3-ols consumed alone, in a banana smoothie, or in a mixed-berry smoothie. The banana smoothie reduced circulating epicatechin metabolites by approximately 80%, whereas the berry smoothie produced levels similar to the flavan-3-ols consumed alone. 

The culprit was polyphenol oxidase, or PPO, an enzyme that oxidizes certain polyphenols when plant tissue is blended. 

- Banana: approximately 3,258 units of PPO activity per 100 grams
- Avocado: approximately 24 units per 100 grams
- Blueberry: approximately 12 units per 100 grams

This does not mean a banana eliminates every beneficial compound in blueberries. Blueberries contain many other polyphenols, including anthocyanins, and this was a small study that should be replicated. But the magnitude of the effect was meaningful enough for me to consider when optimizing my smoothie. 

My solution is simple: I replace the banana with avocado. 
 
Per 100 grams, avocado contains approximately 95% less sugar, more than twice the fiber, about 36% more potassium, and more folate, vitamin K, and niacin than banana. It also contains substantially more monounsaturated fat (and therefore more calories) which may not align with everyone’s goals. 
 
For me, that fat is another advantage. I add kale to my smoothie, which is rich in lutein. Lutein accumulates in the retina and the brain, where it contributes to visual and cognitive function. Human studies have found that adding avocado to a carotenoid-rich meal can substantially increase lutein (more than 5-fold) and beta-carotene absorption. 

So this is not about labeling bananas as “bad.” It is about matching the ingredient to the objective, which is polyphenol optimization (for me).

caption:
THE AGITATION FROM ERRORS THAT ACCOMPANIES YOUR GENUINE ATTEMPTS TO DO SOMETHING NEW ARE WHAT TRIGGER NEUROPLASTICITY & LEARNING •

Excerpt from @joerogan @joeroganexperience podcast out now @spotifypodcasts where we discussed how (and why, at a biological level) doing hard things makes doing other hard things feel easier, let’s you access more appreciation and leads to a sense of peace. 

We also discussed how some degree of frustration from making errors while trying to learn is a *necessary* component of stable learning. 

Most people back away from that agitation. But it literally reflects the release of neuromodulators that tell your brain connections to change. 

Understanding this fact can help you learn anything faster. Recognize what the agitation is and that, in the context of learning, it’s a good thing. You don’t want to be overly stressed, but you need to be agitated and focused on the task at hand. And making errors through genuine attempts. 

Forget learning in a flow state. There is no learning in flow and there is no flow in learning. Flow is the expression of what you already can do.

Our discussion also covered mental health from different perspectives, why it took me eight years and four complete rewrites before finally releasing my book Protocols, and much more.

This is a big deal. Omega-3s reduce aggressive behavior across randomized controlled trials.

A meta-analysis of 29 studies and nearly 4,000 participants found that omega-3 supplementation reduced aggressive behavior by up to 28%. The benefit was broadly consistent across children and adults, males and females, community and clinical samples, and across high and low omega-3 doses and treatment durations. It also helped with both reactive/impulsive and proactive/planned aggression.

Mechanistically, this makes sense. Omega-3s are deeply involved in brain cell membranes, neurotransmission, neuroinflammation, cerebral blood flow, and gene regulation. DHA is especially enriched in the prefrontal cortex, which is critical for impulse control, emotion regulation, and executive function.

The authors even concluded that there is now “sufficient evidence” to begin implementing omega-3 supplementation to reduce aggression in the community, the clinic, or the criminal justice system. That’s a remarkable statement for a nutritional intervention and a reminder that omega-3s influence brain health and may also shape behavior in meaningful ways.

Study title:
“Omega-3 supplementation reduces aggressive behavior: A meta-analytic review of randomized controlled trials”

caption:
Nicotine can enhance cognition, but it comes at a cost to cardiovascular health.

A single 2–4 mg nicotine pouch can raise blood pressure by ~5 mmHg and increase resting heart rate by ~5–10 beats per minute. Higher doses lead to more pronounced elevations.

More concerning is nicotine’s effect on arterial stiffness, which is a marker strongly associated with long-term cardiovascular disease risk.

These effects are driven largely by nicotine’s activation of the sympathetic nervous system, which promotes vasoconstriction and impairs endothelial function.

While the cardiovascular effects are often short-lived, repeated exposure can make them persistent in habitual users.

I talked about nicotine as well as supplements for cancer, inflammation, and general health and well-being with @missmayim on her podcast earlier this year.

alt: Video by Peter Attia, M.D. on September 05, 2025.

caption:
IMPROVE IMPULSE CONTROL •

Human learning (many forms anyway), and canine training are fundamentally not that different. At least at the level of neuroscience. 

All mammals, have a patch of brain called the prefrontal cortex. It has a bunch of different functions and subregions, but one of its main functions is to help you learn and implement specific strategies in specific contexts. 

Early in life all mammals learn top-down-inhibition: which is the suppression of impulses by, among other things, the prefrontal cortex. 

All mammals, including humans have a diminished ability to do this when we are sleep deprived or if we’ve been doing it a lot— the system fatigues. 

that’s why it’s hard to hold your focused attention on something for many many hours unless there’s a lot of novelty updates in what you’re trying to focus on.

That fatigue, induced reduction and prefrontal cortical inhibition is also the basis for “zoomies” (in dogs), why it’s hard for young kids to sit still, and why many adults run out of patience. 

Humans have leveraged top@down inhibition to teach domestic animals how to do certain things like run on treadmills or sit for a treat. There are other things involved too, but it’s central to the process.

In our own lives, our prefrontal cortex is constantly updating what we think of as reasonable or unreasonable impulses to express in a given context. 

And people with damage to this brain area tend to show context inappropriate behaviors. 

The coolest part: learning top down inhibition of impulse control is context dependent, but your ability to express impulse control does get built up like a muscle that you train.

This is why self discipline builds on itself, and allows you to be functional in more areas of life than the place where you built the self discipline.

OK, that’s enough neuroscience and food for thought. Have a great weekend! 

And thank you for your interest in science!

caption:
This past week I stepped away from my normal routine and spent a couple days hiking through the Grand Canyon and the red rock desert of Sedona with my family. No notifications. No news cycle. Just thousands of feet of elevation change, warm sun, cold mornings, tired legs, and a very visceral reminder of how precious it is to have a body and a family healthy enough to do this together. On a day that is about gratitude, I am thankful for that.

Long nature hikes have many health benefits. Mechanical loading on muscles and bones, mitochondrial biogenesis driven by energetic demands, intense natural light exposure resetting circadian rhythms, and visually immersive natural environments quieting the brain’s rumination-prone default-mode network.

Yet, what I value most deeply is the shared effort and hardship with my family, especially teaching my son that strength emerges directly from struggle. There were parts of our hikes that were more challenging and hard. True adaptation requires stress. Stress in the muscles, mitochondria, even the mind itself, all grow stronger in response to challenge. Without hardship, there can be no meaningful growth. This was the most valuable lesson that I continue to instill in my son.

Today I’m especially thankful for my health, for the health of my family, and for the ability to share these kinds of experiences with them. Wishing you and your loved ones a healthy, peaceful, and restorative Thanksgiving.

caption:
INSPIRATION, DAILY EFFORT & (NO) EXCUSES •
-
This is the 90 year old grandfather of @gasmoney1 doing 20 pushups, and check the form! He even pauses mid-set to rib one of his kids/grandkids about their partial rep tendencies. Ha!
-
I saw this when @gasmoney1 posted it (he has some great content on life design and aligning your work with deep meaning etc) and in addition to the impressive nature of the physical output of his 90 year old grandfather, a couple other things are extra cool/inspiring about it. 

1) he’s with family. A lot of people will see fitness stuff online and start saying “oh this is all they do” etc. but I encourage people pursue physical health and performance in the context of a full healthy life. It’s not in either-or. @athleanx @jockowillink @ken_rideout @cameronrhanes @drgabriellelyon = just few examples of those that have that balance And now @jellyroll615 too! (His transformation is !!!). 

2) @gasmoney1 told me that his grandfather just “does something physical every day”; and he still works. I dont know if he spent time in the gym (maybe, I didn’t ask but ), but he certainly puts in physical effort and has for his entire life. Daily investment pays off. 

3) He is laughing and having fun while pushing. This is so vital. When I was in my teens, the best advice I got about exercise was “learn to enjoy training really hard”. 

I internalized that and I also applied it to school and work and yes, you still need to learn how to relax and recreate! but you really can learn to enjoy working hard. As my colleague @draliacrum at Stanford says “a mindset is a setting for your brain” (so simple but so apt!)… a hard work is fun mindset will make your life so much better. 
-
So… anytime you’re thinking about making an excuse about physical exercise or find yourself resenting hard work, remember this guy pushing out 20 push-ups at 90! Surrounded by family. Joyfully.

I start with the fundamentals.

Beware of most creatine gummies. Recent third-party testing found that 2/3 of creatine gummy brands contained virtually no creatine, despite label claims.

Gummies are often a bad delivery system in general, not just for creatine. Manufacturing heat and processing can degrade sensitive compounds and reduce biological activity. You’re also paying for sugar, fillers, and convenience, not potency.

Plus, if you’re aiming for a meaningful daily dose (e.g., 10–20 g/day), that’s a lot of gummies.

Creatine monohydrate powder is still the gold standard for those who want to supplement.

How Much Exercise Is Really Enough for Longevity?

This clip is from the video “How much time should a person spend exercising?“ which was released on my YouTube channel on 5/4/24.

“How much time do I need to spend exercising?” It’s a question I hear often, and it is the subject of countless research studies and popular press articles. And yet, this question misses the point.

When it comes to exercise, we should only concern ourselves with duration insofar as it influences what we really care about: results. Exercise is not a goal in itself – rather, it is a means of achieving good cardiorespiratory fitness, strength, and metabolic health, and the ultimate indicators of sufficient exercise are therefore a good VO2 max and adequate muscle mass.

caption:
You asked for Part 2... unfortunately, the food industry delivered.

I wish I could tell you these were fake products generated by AI.

But they’re not.

These are actual products being sold in grocery stores across America right now.

Dr Pepper sausage. Fried chicken jelly beans. Birthday cake coffee creamer. Rocket Pop baked beans.

Big Food is literally competing to make products more addictive, more profitable, and more impossible to ignore.

And once again, flip these packages over and you’ll find many of the same ingredients:

• Artificial food dyes linked to behavioral concerns in children.
• Emulsifiers like polysorbate 80, carboxymethylcellulose, carrageenan, and mono- & diglycerides that may disrupt the gut microbiome and intestinal barrier.
• “Natural flavors”—a catch-all term that can represent dozens of undisclosed flavoring compounds.
• Refined starches, high-fructose corn syrup, maltodextrin, preservatives, gums, and additives engineered to maximize shelf life and keep you coming back for more.

Food should nourish us.

Instead, we’ve normalized products that are essentially marketing experiments wrapped in colorful packaging.

We deserve better than food designed by branding teams instead of biology.

caption:
When I was 35, I went from being able to ride my bike 100 miles to struggling to walk up a flight of stairs. I was exhausted, couldn’t sleep, and had brain fog so severe I would lose my train of thought halfway through a sentence.

I was a doctor, and I couldn’t figure out what was happening to my own body.

That experience changed the way I practiced medicine. It made me more curious about what my patients were experiencing, and more determined to understand why they were sick.

Over decades of caring for patients, I’ve learned how much it matters to ask about the everyday details of someone’s life. What are they eating? Are they sleeping? Do they have time to rest? What has happened to them? Those questions belong in the exam room.

Food, movement, and rest are part of how we care for a body that is working hard to keep us alive. They deserve our attention, even when healing also requires medical treatment and a deeper search for answers.

And when you’ve felt unwell for a long time, having a place to begin can mean everything.

You don’t have to overhaul your life today. Start with one meal you make for yourself. Give yourself the same patience and care you would offer someone you love.

If you don’t know where to start, start with what you eat. Drop a YES below and I’ll DM you a link to my FREE Nutrition 101 PDF.

Vigorous intensity physical activity is 4–10x more effective than moderate activity for reducing the risk of major chronic diseases.

One minute of vigorous activity offers roughly the same reduction in all-cause mortality risk as 4 minutes of moderate activity. When looking closer at specific outcomes, the impact becomes even clearer.

For cardiovascular mortality, you’d need about 8 minutes of moderate activity to equal just one minute at vigorous intensity; for type 2 diabetes, it’s closer to 10 minutes. In terms of cancer-related mortality, again, vigorous activity proves four times more potent than moderate intensity.

These findings are eye-opening, but perhaps not surprising when we consider the superior cardiovascular and metabolic adaptations in response to vigorous-intensity activity, including better cardiorespiratory fitness and insulin sensitivity.

Learn more about the benefits of vigorous activity in the latest FoundMyFitness episode - The Best Type of Exercise for Longevity.

caption:
A note to myself:
The Sun is rising for me
The Moon is shining for me
The wind is blowing for me
The rain is raining for me
The snow is snowing for me
The sea is breathing for me
The sand is getting warm for me
The flowers are blooming for me
The birds are singing for me
The music is created for me to dance to it

Everything here exists to entertain my senses. This world is created for me to FEEL it.

And yet, all of that serves as a trap. This planet is a venus flytrap for souls. We're seduced by its beauty, but more than that we're seduced by the opportunity to experience the most incredible thing - physical love. That is the actual bait souls are caught by. To kiss your child, to hug your lover, to be held by your parent, to laugh with your best friend- all of that is so tempting you can't resist it. So you incarnate in this realm, and bam💥- welcome to the world of suffering disguised as love and beauty to enjoy all of the above before it is taken from you. So cruel!

Feel free to borrow that note and keep it as a reminder. 
Don't waist your time, enjoy all of that while you can, even though there's underlying bitterness of a loss present in every second of your life here.
It's eased when you are able to generate that love from inside yourself and shower Your Self with it. Nothing is as liberating and invigorating as self-love.

caption:
Magnesium is one of the most evidence-backed supplements for treating migraine.

400–600 mg per day of oral magnesium reduces migraine frequency and intensity vs placebo in randomized trials. Some studies find benefit only at the higher end (600 mg/day) while lower doses (250–360 mg) often fail to help.

For acute attacks, IV magnesium can also be effective, particularly for migraines with aura.

Magnesium stabilizes neuronal membranes (reducing brain hyper-excitability) and modulates cerebral vascular tone, two core processes in migraine biology.

For routine supplementation, magnesium glycinate, citrate or taurate are preferred for bioavailability. Magnesium threonate gets attention for brain uptake, but it contains very little elemental magnesium and should not replace more bioavailable forms when your goal is correcting total magnesium status.

Another evidence-based regimen for migraine prevention is combining magnesium with CoQ10 and riboflavin (B2), which reduced migraine days substantially in a 3-month trial.

If GI upset is a problem, split the total into ~200 mg doses taken 1–3×/day. This keeps you in the 400–600 mg/day range shown to be effective while reducing loose stools.

4. Mechanisms are textbook, not proven. 
Stabilizing membranes? Modulating tone? Great theory. But this study never tested those mechanisms. Citing broken stats as proof of biology is a logical leap, not evidence.

Bottom line: 
One flawed meta-analysis ≠ clinical fact. Don’t let bad math dictate your treatment.

caption:
A woman lived to 117 without cancer, cardiovascular disease, or neurodegenerative disease. Then scientists examined nearly every layer of her biology.

The results are incredibly cool.

María Branyas Morera showed unmistakable signs of extreme age. Her telomeres were the shortest among the healthy people studied, her blood contained age-related clonal hematopoiesis mutations, and her immune cells carried an aged signature.

But other parts of her biology looked remarkably youthful:

• Her epigenetic age was approximately 23 years younger than her chronological age
• She had exceptionally efficient lipid metabolism, with very low triglycerides and VLDL cholesterol and high HDL cholesterol
• Her systemic inflammation was strikingly low
• She carried rare genetic variants linked to immune fitness, cardiovascular protection, brain health, and mitochondrial function
• Her gut microbiome was unusually diverse and enriched in Bifidobacterium—a beneficial genus that typically declines with age

She also followed a Mediterranean diet, ate plenty of yogurt, walked, gardened, read, played piano, slept well, and maintained an active social life.

What I find most fascinating is that her biology looked profoundly old in some ways and surprisingly young in others. She may offer us a glimpse of how aging and disease can become uncoupled.

This is one exceptional person, so it isn’t a longevity formula. But cases like hers can reveal which systems may be especially important to preserve as we age, including metabolic health, immune resilience, low inflammation, a healthy microbiome, and continued physical and social engagement.

caption:
Supplementing with protein during strength training can increase gains in muscle size by approximately 27%, even when baseline protein intake is already considered adequate.

The current RDA for protein, 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight per day, is meant to prevent deficiency, not to optimize muscle growth or performance. Increasing intake to 1.5x the RDA leads to greater improvements in both muscle size and strength when combined with resistance exercise.

Doubling the RDA is even better. Meta-analyses suggest that around 1.6 g/kg/day of protein is sufficient to maximize gains in muscle strength and fat-free mass, with potential (though smaller) benefits observed at higher intakes up to 2.2 g/kg/day for those aiming to fully optimize muscle growth and recovery (like athletes).

This highlights how conservative the RDA truly is and why higher protein intakes are important, particularly for individuals engaging in regular strength training or other forms of physical activity.

caption:
Having your last meal at least 3 hours before bed improves blood pressure, heart health, and even blood glucose regulation.

Participants who stopped eating 3+ hours before sleep (extending their overnight fast to 13-16 hours) improved overnight diastolic blood pressure dipping by 3.5% and overnight heart rate by 5%. They also had a higher (better) HRV, lower cortisol, and improved insulin sensitivity.

That was without changing what or how much they ate!

This is one strategy I’ve advocated for years, so it’s promising to see further support from a controlled study on “sleep-aligned” eating patterns.

What you eat matters. But so does when.

caption:
We have been taught to think of health as something we deal with after it is gone.

We wait for the diagnosis, then try to manage the disease.

But chronic disease often develops quietly for years before it is given a name. The food you eat, the quality of your sleep, how often you move, your exposure to chronic stress, and the health of your relationships all influence your biology long before symptoms become severe.

This does not mean every illness is preventable or that medical treatment is unnecessary. Modern medicine is extraordinary at treating infections, trauma, emergencies, and advanced disease.

But creating health requires more than treating symptoms.

It means understanding why dysfunction developed, addressing the root causes, and building the conditions that allow the body to function at its best.

Your genes are not always your destiny. Your symptoms are not inconveniences to ignore. And your daily choices are more powerful than you may realize.

The best time to care for your health is not after a diagnosis.

It is now.

HAPPY 4th July and 250th Birthday USA •
-
Forever grateful to be born in this incredible country.

When you grow up the child of a first generation immigrant— as I did, you hear all the time about how incredible it is here, what aspects of it do and don’t exist elsewhere and how lucky we are to live here. 

The USA has a history of being supportive of science and engineering. That’s what brought my father here. My mother was already an American citizen. I am so grateful for their experiment that was me (and my siblings). 

And while that is my story and perspective … let’s not forget we are all mutts… there are no true pure breeds. … In fact, nature punishes that with deleterious mutations. 

So, despite all the divisiveness that exists nowadays, I remain optimistic that we will move this experiment forward toward the outcomes that continue to provide the most freedom and liberty for the greatest number of people …as long as they honor the freedoms and liberties of other people. That can be a complicated equation sometimes. But we can do it. We’ve made it this far. 

And for those of you not from the United States, every time I travel, I see aspects of other countries that I think we would be wise to incorporate here. That’s the whole point. This USA thing is an experiment and a relatively young one. It is still happening. We are the experiment. 

A couple of final points:
I don’t use a teleprompter. I never have here or on the podcast. Except for ad reads, of course where the language has to be precise down to the word, but I don’t blink much… that’s how I remember when I want to say. So ditch the notion that this is a teleprompter post or political in any way. I truly love this country and I’m a patriot. And I’m proud to say it. 

Wishing you all a happy and safe Fourth of July. Let’s keep moving this experiment forward!

“FACE PULLS”: SET YOUR DEFAULT POSTURE UPRIGHT, MAKE YOUR SHOULDERS AND NECK STABLE •

This week’s Huberman Lab podcast features Jeff Cavalier of  @athleanx — he’s a licensed physical therapist, strength and conditioning coach known for helping people reach their fitness goals, overcoming pain and injury with specific movements and getting tremendous longevity from their fitness training. 

We sat down and talked about “the little things that allow you to do the big important things for your entire life” on the podcast. 

Yes it’s true: You need to do the basics. Men and women should do basic compound movements of pressing and pulling and for their legs …and do so with progressive resistance. Every week. 

But the issue people tend to run into is pain or injuries or challenges with imbalanced mechanics. Doing certain little things for just a few minutes per week can be the difference between lifelong pain-free training, great posture (at default— without having to think about it!) better breathing, better mobility, and on and on.

One of the key movements that every man and woman should do a few times a week at least are “face pulls” which is where you pull a rope from slightly above high-level on a cable machine (or you could use bands if you don’t have access to a cable machine) starting from a position where your hands are almost touching directly in front of you (arms straight) to what sort of looks like a “double biceps flexed pose”, but with your thumbs pointed back and  bit out & away from your ears. That’s the correct “external rotation” you want, which is essential… you can learn more about on the podcast. 

All the texting and sitting that we do nowadays has most people defaulting to internal rotation, chin down and C shaped… not good (for many reasons!).

A video of how to do face pulls correctly as well as train your arms correctly are available at the “Huberman lab clips” channel on You Tube. There is a short excerpt of it here as well.

Thank you, Jeff for being such a tremendous coach in public educator helping people get and stay super fit. We appreciate you!

caption:
Dad’s workouts may shape his child’s endurance capacity and metabolic health.

Not by passing on mitochondria—which come from mom—but by sending tiny sperm microRNA messages that tune early embryonic gene regulation.

In a new study (mice), exercising fathers produced offspring with a higher VO2 max, greater endurance, a leaner body composition, and more mitochondria. They also had superior glucose control and insulin sensitivity when challenged with a high-fat diet.

Effects tracked to sperm small RNAs that suppressed a “molecular brake” on PGC-1α, the classic mitochondrial biogenesis switch.

This reframes preconception health as a two-parent story: mom supplies the mitochondria, but dad’s training status can still program how those mitochondria are used.

Study referenced - DOI: 10.1016/j.cmet.2025.09.003

caption:
NEUROPLASTICITY: THE 4 STEPS TO LEARNING •
-
STEP 1: ALERTNESS 
Aside from developmental plasticity, which sets up basic sensory functions like our ability to see and hear, etc., all forms of neuroplasticity  and learning require us to be alert. That is, in a state of slightly (or greatly) elevated autonomic arousal. But if arousal is too high, the next step doesn’t happen and it must….

2) FOCUS 
It is an absolute truth that whatever we focus our perceptual attention on is what stands the best chance to be remembered. That could be a process, a fact, a contingency like when and how often rewards arrive or punishments arrive… all of that shapes behavior. (by the way if you’re wondering what the best reward schedule is, it’s intermittent… ~random reward intervals. 

3) AGITATION (FROM ERRORS!)
This is the hardest one for people to embrace. In the absence of errors, your nervous system has no reason to change. Please read that twice. 

But why? What do errors actually do? They change the neurochemical environment in the areas of your nervous system that need to change. You need to embrace the agitation that comes from errors. That doesn’t mean you need to be stressed, but you need to feel enough agitation that it allows you to dial your focus in deeper on the things you’re trying to learn.

4) SLEEP & TIME
The rewiring of your nervous system largely takes place during sleep. In particular, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. That form of sleep that predominates the last 1/3rd of your night. If you want to rewire your brain: for new skills, to alter your emotional relationship to an experience of past or in the present or future anticipated experience, you need the sleep that comes the night after learning attempts.

We do treadmill training twice a day. He’s doing it for intermittent reinforcement. Eventually reward will come at the end. He learned selfies the first time.

Incandescent bulbs tend to be full spectrum meaning they emit short, medium, and long wavelengths. That is good because the long wavelengths improve your mitochondria and offset what appears to be the damage of short wavelengths. 
-
Sunlight, of course, is full spectrum. So getting sunlight in your eyes and on your skin each day can help offset some of the mitochondrial damage being done by LED bulbs.

caption:
PLEASE WELCOME… STRUMMER. 
(Named after the Great @joestrummer of course; the Clash, Mescaleros) 

Strummer is 10 weeks old today. 

This is my second Olde English Bulldog. For those of you that have listened to the podcast for a while you may recall early episodes that featured Costello — also an Olde English Bulldog (which is distinct from pure English bulldog; Olde English are mutted with Mastiff and Pit, which yields pups that breathe better and move better). Costello passed (after a long life) in 2021. 

Strummer’s morning routine:
Wake up
Sunlight
Walk 
Training (yes we started training him right away. He can already Sit. Stay. Wait. And he knows to make eye contact. He’s learning most things in two trials… he’s very smart). We only use rewards and semi-intermittent reinforcement to train. 

Then we do a little bit of nose training: then… Free play. 
Then he eats breakfast. 
Water.
And then he gets a nap in front of a red incandescent light @saunaspace (no affiliation, but theirs are amazing.)

We repeat that routine in the evening.

Obviously, he does not need @mateina — the Yerba zero sugar, cold brew organic mate I helped develop, but I DO! (And I drink the loose leaf Mateina Yerba too, brewed hot). 

A few bulldog facts:

The Olde English line from the early last century and 1800s used for bullbaiting (thankfully a banned sport now) is different than the line that was revitalized in the 1970s, but the idea is similar: healthier bulldog breed, better breathing. 

Why?
Well, English bulldogs are wonderful animals, but excessive inbreeding has caused a lot of problems for the breed over the last 30 years. People get them and they don’t realize how much work and cost they are and the many medical problems that go with that inbreeding, such as apnea etc. The @bulldogclubofamerica & @americankennelclub breeders are working hard to restore health to the pure English Bulldog breed.

And I purposefully kept his tail! 
Let it wag!

PS: As with Costello, my good friend Elvis Cortez—  Left Alone, @hellcatrecords & member of @thetransplantsband found Strummer for me. Elvis, thank you!

caption:
Higher meat intake was associated with less cognitive decline and lower dementia risk in APOE e4 carriers, a group at higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease and dementia.

Those who ate ~2 servings of meat per day had a better 10-year cognitive trajectory and a 55% lower dementia risk compared to people eating less than a half a serving per day.

That pattern wasn’t seen in the non-APOE e4 carriers and was NOT observed for processed meat. Unprocessed red meat alone was also linked to lower dementia risk in APOE e4 carriers.

My take is not “everyone should eat more meat.”

But a few servings per day of unprocessed meat (as observed in this study) is perfectly healthy for most people.

caption:
Hitting a wall during your workouts? Getting that awful afternoon brain fog that coffee just can't fix? It might be time to look at what's happening inside your body, specifically, your iron levels. 🏃‍♀️📉

Think of iron as a delivery truck for your oxygen. It helps your blood carry oxygen straight to your muscles and your brain. When your iron levels start to drop, your body is essentially running on empty.

Why tracking this matters for your energy:
🍽️ Iron helps your body turn the food you eat into real, usable energy.
📉Low iron means you get tired faster, your heart has to work harder, and it takes longer to recover after a tough workout.
🎯Your brain needs constant oxygen to think clearly. When iron is low, it’s much harder to focus.

➡️If you are already tracking your sleep, your steps, and your food, make sure you are tracking your blood data, too. Getting healthy always starts from the inside out. 🩸✨

#FitnessTips #IronHealth #TrackYourHealth

caption:
The current physical activity guidelines are too low.

I’ve been saying this for a while. And a new study confirms it.

Meeting the standard 150 minutes/week was associated with only a modest ~8–9% lower cardiovascular risk.

The biggest protection occurred at roughly 560–610 minutes/week, about 3–4× higher, where cardiovascular risk was 30% lower.

One other interesting finding was that people with a higher cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2 max) needed less activity than people with lower fitness to achieve the same reduction in risk!

You’re never too old to start building muscle.

Muscle acts as a metabolic reservoir, storing and utilizing glucose efficiently, preventing insulin resistance, and protecting against chronic disease. The study found that muscle mass—not BMI—was the strongest predictor of survival, independent of fat mass, cardiovascular risk factors, and metabolic markers.

I used to think lifting weights was just for bodybuilders—I didn’t love the gym and thought cardio was enough. But when I learned that strength training activates longevity pathways like mTOR and AMPK, protects mitochondria, and triggers the release of myokines—hormone-like compounds that reduce inflammation and enhance brain function—I realized it wasn’t just about looking fit. It was about living longer, stronger, and healthier.

You don’t need a gym or fancy equipment. Strength training—whether it’s bodyweight exercises, resistance bands, or lifting weights—builds muscle, protects your metabolic health, and safeguards your future.

At the end of the day, it’s not just about living longer—it’s about living better.

caption:
You may be paying a premium for avocado oil and getting cheaper oils instead.

A new UC Davis study found that 48 of 54 processed foods labeled with avocado oil, or 89%, also contained other oils such as canola and safflower.

Every salad dressing tested failed purity checks, along with 93% of chips and 71% of mayonnaises.

Importantly, this does not necessarily mean the brands knowingly misled consumers. Many food manufacturers purchase oils through third-party brokers or multiple suppliers. Lead researcher Selina Wang believes the adulteration likely begins with suppliers who blend avocado oil with less expensive oils before selling it as pure.

But brands still have a responsibility to test and verify the ingredients they purchase.

So what can you do?

Prioritize whole, minimally processed foods. Read the complete ingredient list instead of relying on front-of-package claims. Look for companies that independently test their oils and verify their suppliers. You can even contact a brand and ask whether it tests its avocado oil for authenticity.

We need stronger purity standards, independent testing, and accountability at every level. If avocado oil is the only oil listed on the label, that is what should be inside.

Source: Lopez-Alvarez et al., Applied Food Research (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.afres.2026.102389

caption:
Using a HEPA air purifier improved performance on a test of executive function by 12% in adults 40 and older... and they only used it for a month!

In this randomized crossover trial, air purifiers were placed in the bedroom and living room. Compared with sham filtration, HEPA filtration reduced indoor PM2.5 by 52% and ultrafine particles by 32%.

I think this matters for several reasons. Inhalation is a major source of microplastic exposure. Tire wear, synthetic clothing, dryer exhaust, shoes, and household dust can all release tiny plastic particles into the air we breathe. The study above didn’t measure microplastics specifically, but HEPA filtration may help reduce exposure to airborne microplastic particles as part of the broader indoor particle load.

Recent research found substantially high concentrations of micro- and nanoplastics in the brain, and even greater accumulation in brains from people with dementia, including Alzheimer’s disease. This association doesn’t prove that microplastics cause dementia, but it adds urgency to understanding and reducing chronic exposure.

An air purifier doesn’t need to be a fancy “medical-grade” model. Choose a HEPA purifier with a clean air delivery rate appropriate for the room, run it consistently in the spaces where you spend the most time, and replace the filter on schedule.

A simple air filter may be one of the most practical ways to reduce the particles we breathe every day. And it’s something I personally do.

caption:
Sitting on the ground more is one of the simplest things you can do for long-term mobility.

It sounds almost too basic, but getting down to the floor and back up is a real marker of independence. If you lose that ability, a lot of everyday function starts to go with it.

Sit with your legs straight out. Sit cross-legged. Kneel. Shift around. These positions gently restore hip rotation, ankle mobility, and the ability to move your body in and out of different shapes.

This kind of low-level, daily movement practice helps maintain better joint mechanics, and according to @thereadystate, it might be one reason why “floor cultures” such as those in Asia often preserve mobility longer and have fewer problems related to stiffness and loss of function.

From the latest episode of the FoundMyFitness podcast. Available on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts.

caption:
Recent research is showing that some of these weight loss drugs GLP-1 receptor agonists, which include Ozempic and things like Wegovy may decrease cancer mortality. The people who are most obese benefit the most.

The effects were big.

Colon cancer patients taking GLP-1 drugs (Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro) were less than half as likely to die within 5 years.

This new study suggests GLP-1 drugs might specifically target obesity-driven inflammatory and metabolic pathways known to accelerate colon cancer progression.

There are several mechanisms by which GLP-1 agonists may suppress tumor growth, including weight loss, improving glucose regulation and insulin sensitivity, and lowering inflammation.

There is also some interesting in-vitro cell culture data indicating that these drugs may directly slow cancer cell proliferation, induce apoptosis, and remodel the tumor microenvironment itself.

So what’s the take-away? Should everyone be on these drugs? Absolutely not. Weight loss is critical. Ideally, diet and lifestyle changes would drive it, but clearly, we’re losing that fight in the US, where obesity contributes to at least 13 types of cancer and many other diseases.

In this study, the greatest benefit from GLP-1 drugs was seen in people with obesity, exactly those who struggle most to lose weight through lifestyle alone.

I think the GLP-1s represent a potential tool, particularly when traditional methods have repeatedly failed some people.

Study title:
The Influence of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists on Five-Year Mortality in Colon Cancer Patients

Preparing for a baby isn’t only about conception but also creating the healthiest possible start for the next generation.

caption:
Using the sauna after aerobic exercise improves VO₂ max more than training alone.

People who performed 30 minutes of cycling and then sat in a sauna for ~15 minutes afterward saw greater gains in their VO₂ max after 8 weeks of training compared to those who did the workout without sauna.

There’s also emerging evidence for strength training, with studies showing greater increases in markers of anabolic signaling associated with muscle growth with post-exercise heat exposure.

The sauna has several health benefits. But it’s also a powerful tool to amplify the body’s adaptations to both endurance and strength training.

You’ve probably never actually calculated how much water you need. Most people haven’t.

The 8-glasses rule isn’t science, it’s a guess that stuck. Your actual number shifts with body size, climate, activity and what’s already on your plate.

caption:
Nobody questions caffeine. It’s just a habit.

Most people have been drinking it the same way since they started. Same time, same amount, never really thinking about it.

Caffeine doesn’t give you energy. It blocks tiredness. When it wears off, the adenosine it’s been suppressing hits all at once. That’s the crash.

Once you understand how caffeine affects your body, you can have it work for you.

caption:
Muscle loss with age is common, but much of that decline is driven by inactivity, not aging alone.

On average, we reach peak muscle mass somewhere between 20 and 30, then lose about 8% per decade after that. By the time many adults reach their 70s and 80s, they may have only 60–80% of the muscle mass they had at 30.

A big reason why is anabolic resistance. As we get older, muscle becomes less responsive to amino acids, one of the key signals for building and maintaining muscle.

This is where resistance training becomes non-negotiable. It’s one of the main signals that tells muscle to grow. And just as importantly, it helps re-sensitize muscle to amino acids, so the body responds to protein more like it did when you were younger.

caption:
A post-workout hot bath enhanced strength gains by nearly 10%, twice the increase observed with a hot shower.

Participants in this study performed high-intensity resistance training a total of five times over two weeks. One group immersed their lower bodies in 40°C (104°F) water for 10 minutes after each workout, while another took a shower at the same temperature.

The bath group saw a 9.3% increase in maximal leg strength—nearly double the 4.5% for the shower group. Baths also reduced peripheral fatigue, supporting better neuromuscular recovery.

Adding light pedaling during immersion offered no additional benefits—the heat stimulus alone appeared to drive adaptations, potentially via heat shock proteins and improved blood flow.

Hot water immersion (via bath or tub) is a simple, accessible way to boost training outcomes for most people. If you have access, a sauna works too!

🛑 Critical Look at the Hot Bath StudyDon't trust the findings blindly. 
The study suggesting hot baths boost muscle gains has significant flaws:
Tiny Sample Size: Only 10 people per group means the study is underpowered. The results are suggestive, not statistically proven (the strength gain wasn't even significant!).
No Blinding: Participants knew if they were taking a hot bath or a cold shower, which creates a huge placebo effect (especially for subjective measures like feeling recovered).
Too Short & Specific: It lasted only two weeks and used only isometric (static) exercise. We can't apply these findings to long-term, dynamic weight training.
Funding Bias: The study was funded by a company that makes water heaters (Rinnai Corporation), introducing a potential conflict of interest.

Bottom line: Interesting idea, but we need much more robust research before changing our recovery routine! 💪

Everything is a mirror—just not always a straightforward one.
Perhaps a courageous soul comes here to experience fear. Deep down, you know you can stand your ground and face whatever comes your way, yet somehow you find yourself doing the opposite. Why? For what purpose?
Maybe simply to discover what it's like to walk in those shoes.
And here's something else to consider:
What is holding you back? What feels like a set of chains around your ankles? What do you believe is preventing you from fully spreading your wings? What limitations are you carrying?
Know this: they are imagined.
Any limitation placed upon your spirit is an illusion you have, for some reason, come to believe.
Seriously—set aside everything else you're reading and look at this book through the eyes of a modern adult.
To me, it feels incredibly relevant right now, at a time when we're being called to face our inner demons. Because this is a pivotal moment.
A moment of returning to our True Nature.
The time is coming when there will be less need to act out old programs, patterns, and roles—to pretend to be someone you are not. What will be required is something much simpler, and perhaps much more challenging:
To be your authentic self.
And if you've never truly known who that self is, then welcome.
These times are inviting us to find out.
The space I create helps my clients look themselves in the eye and gaze into their own souls.
And do you know the best part?
When people dare to look within, they discover their strength. ✨

caption:
International travel finally caught up with me, so yesterday became a bone broth day.

After a stretch of flights, time-zone changes, and disrupted sleep, I woke up feeling a little worn down. 

Not terribly sick, but enough that my body was asking for warmth, fluids, and a slower pace.

Bone broth is one of my go-tos on days like this because it’s simple and deeply nourishing. Warm fluids, protein, collagen-derived gelatin, and amino acids like glycine and proline from a long, slow simmer. I also like adding ginger and turmeric for the flavor, warmth, and the anti-inflammatory compounds they contain.

Here’s the version I made:

• 2–3 lbs beef bones, ideally marrow + joint bones
• 3–4 inches fresh ginger, sliced
• 2–3 inches fresh turmeric, sliced
• 2 tbsp apple cider vinegar
• 1 large onion, quartered
• 1 head garlic, halved or smashed
• Optional: carrots + celery
• 1 tbsp whole black peppercorns
• 1–2 bay leaves
• 1 tsp sea salt
• 8–10 cups water, enough to cover everything

Roast the bones at 400°F for 30 minutes, until deeply browned.

Transfer to a slow cooker with the remaining ingredients.

Cover with water and cook on LOW for 12–24 hours.

Strain, cool, skim excess fat if desired, and store in the fridge.

I’ll be sipping this over the next few days while doing the boring-but-important recovery things like sleep, hydration, sunlight, and taking it easy until I feel fully back.

caption:
My friend @hubermanlab just sounded the alarm on the coolest hack for falling back asleep.

If you wake up in the middle of the night, keep your eyes closed, move them slowly side to side, circle them counterclockwise, then clockwise, then cross them toward your nose and take a long, slow exhale. Repeat until you drift off.

It sounds strange, but there’s real biology behind it.

To fall asleep, your brain has to stop tracking where your body is in space. Your eyes are wired into your balance system, so moving them in slow, unfamiliar patterns scrambles those signals and your brain lets go. 

The side-to-side motion also quiets the amygdala, your brain’s threat center, and the long exhale slows your heart rate and shifts you into rest.

One more thing. If you’re waking up at the same time every night, it’s worth asking why. Blood sugar dips, alcohol close to bedtime, high stress hormones, and light in the bedroom are common culprits. This trick helps you get back to sleep. Fixing the root cause helps you stay there.

Try it next time you’re up in the middle of the night, and let us know if it worked!

caption:
The strength you build today helps determine how you’ll live decades from now.

These illustrations show a cross-section of the thigh. Red represents muscle, pale tissue represents fat, and the structure near the center is the femur. They illustrate how strength training can help preserve muscle as we age. 

Why is this so important?

Muscle is one of your body’s largest destinations for glucose. When you use it, it takes up sugar from your bloodstream to help fuel movement. Regular resistance training can improve insulin sensitivity and blood sugar control, even without weight loss. 

Muscle also gives you the capacity to move through your life. Building and maintaining strength helps protect mobility and independence.

Aging brings real biological changes, but your body can still respond to training later in life. You can build strength in your 60s, 70s, and beyond. I didn’t start until I was 59, and now I’m in the best shape of my life at 66!

Start with two days of strength training each week. Use weights, machines, resistance bands, or bodyweight exercises that challenge you with good form, and gradually increase the demand as you get stronger.

Think about the life you want to be able to live at 80. The places you want to go… The people you want to keep up with. The things you want to do for yourself. 

Every time you train, you’re investing in that future. 🙏

caption:
Drink your coffee black (no additives) if you want the full health benefits. ☕️

2-3 cups per day has been associated with a 25% reduction in all-cause mortality. That benefit goes away when cream and/or sugar are added.

I think this happens for a few reasons:

• Dairy proteins can bind to coffee’s antioxidants and polyphenols and slow their absorption.

• Heavy cream, butter, and MCT-heavy coffee don’t necessarily block coffee polyphenols, but they can add substantial saturated fat and calories. For someone watching ApoB or LDL-C, this can work against the very cardiovascular benefits they’re hoping to get from coffee.

caption:
You could be 40 or 50 years away from knowing whether your habits paid off. Or you could look at your walking pace right now.

A new study followed nearly 4,000 adults in their 80s and found that the fastest walkers, people moving quicker than 93 percent of their peers, were 50 percent less likely to develop cognitive impairment, and 60 percent less likely to be diagnosed with Alzheimer’s or another dementia. Brain scans backed it up: these fast walkers had slower memory decline and better-preserved hippocampal volume, the brain region most tied to memory.

Walking briskly requires your brain, heart, lungs, and nervous system to coordinate in real time. Losing that coordination may be one of the earliest signs your brain is changing.

Luckily gait speed is trainable. Focus on cadence, not just stride. Add short bursts of brisk walking a few times a week. Strengthen your hips and core. Swing your arms.

Swipe through to see the full study, and what to start doing today.

Could cancer become largely curable within the next decade?

Cancer is not one disease, but hundreds, and one reason it’s so difficult to treat is that cancer cells arise from our own tissues. Destroying them without harming healthy cells requires extraordinary precision.

AI may help make that precision possible by integrating genetics, metabolism, immune function, and enormous biological datasets to identify the vulnerabilities unique to each tumor. We are already seeing the beginnings of this with targeted drugs designed around specific mutations and CAR-T therapies that engineer immune cells to recognize and destroy cancer.

A provocative (and hopeful) forecast from @derya_unutmaz_md.

caption:
I want you to eat blueberries, just not with bananas (unless you really want to).

In my new episode, I examine the evidence for blueberries’ benefits on blood flow, brain aging, glucose regulation, gut health, inflammation, and exercise recovery.

Blueberries improve the ability of arteries to relax and deliver blood to the brain, heart, and working muscles. They can improve insulin sensitivity and buffer the blood-sugar response to a calorie-rich meal. Human interventions have also demonstrated improved aspects of memory and cognition in older adults, while observational data link regular blueberry intake to slower cognitive decline.

This isn’t simply an antioxidant story. Blueberry polyphenols act like biological signals, influencing nitric oxide, inflammation, gene expression, and possibly neuronal plasticity.

I also revisit the controversial banana-smoothie question, and explain why I take a cautious approach when my goal is maximizing blueberry-polyphenol exposure.

The full episode is out now on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts. Enjoy!

These are the supplements I give my aging parents:

• A daily multivitamin
• Vitamin D
• High-DHA omega-3s
• Ubiquinol (the reduced form of CoQ10)
• Sulforaphane

Why these?

Large RCTs show improved cognition in older adults taking a standard multivitamin, with benefits equivalent to a brain that’s 2-5 years younger.

For vitamin D, more than 70% of older U.S. adults are insufficient, and aging skin produces far less vitamin D from sunlight (a 70-year-old makes roughly 4x less than their 20-year-old self).

DHA is a key structural fat in the brain and supports cognitive function, especially important with aging and neurodegenerative risk, while CoQ10 supports mitochondrial energy production as levels drop with age.

Finally, sulforaphane is a powerful activator of Nrf2, the body’s master stress-response pathway, up-regulating glutathione and phase II detox enzymes.

Today is the Autumn Equinox.
You may have noticed that I always write about these days. There are only four of them each year — two solstices and two equinoxes — and I feel that each of these celestial turning points has an influence on us.
Today, day and night are equal. From here, the days will gradually become shorter, and we are entering a new season — autumn and winter.
Nature is recalibrating, and we do the same.
Today is a good day to look within a little more closely. To bring your systems back into balance, especially your mental and emotional ones.
Ask yourself: What do I want to take with me into this next season? What am I ready to leave behind? What is no longer supporting my wellbeing?
And perhaps, before looking at external circumstances, look at your own patterns, beliefs and ways of responding.
Not “Who or what is getting in my way?” but “How am I showing up in this situation? How am I showing up in my relationships?”
It can also be a beautiful day for a little clearing and renewal. Clean your home. Let go of things you no longer need. Take a conscious shower and imagine the water washing away whatever has been weighing on you, while you welcome — with gratitude — whatever new and nourishing the flow of life is bringing.
Spend some time in silence and solitude. Listen to yourself. Listen to the space around you.
In other words, the Autumn Equinox can be a wonderful point for a reset, recalibration and rebalancing.
Do whatever feels right for you. All kinds of simple rituals and practices can be helpful, especially when life feels less peaceful or settled than you would like.
For me, it feels particularly important today to listen to myself and to the space around me, and to recalibrate my own systems.
I can sense a certain turbulence around me — not necessarily something coming from me. People around me are going through their own storms, I’ve been holding space for them, and there have also been a few unexpected events (fortunately, with good outcomes).
So yes, this feels like an important day.
A turning point.
The beginning of another season of our lives.
Wishing you a gentle transition and a smooth landing into autumn and winter. 🍁🍀

caption:
A “plastic-free diet” can cut endocrine-disrupting chemicals in the body by up to 60% in just 1 week.

Participants in a recent study switched to low-plastic food, plastic-free kitchenware, and screened personal care products for 7 days.

Urinary BPA fell by 59%, and phthalates fell by up to 54%. Even switching personal care products alone significantly lowered MnBP, another phthalate, by 35%.

These chemicals have been linked to male and female reproductive problems, altered neurodevelopment in children, and even insulin resistance and cardiovascular disease.

The takeaway here is that exposure to plastic is not fixed or unavoidable. Reducing highly processed foods, canned foods, plastic packaging, and plastic contact during food prep and storage, as well as personal hygiene products that contain phthalates, can rapidly lower your internal burden of these chemicals.

Study title: Low-plastic diet and urinary levels of plastic-associated phthalates and bisphenols: the randomized controlled PERTH Trial

Some moments don’t just move you — they change you. 

A sense of awe is what truly impacts your immune system. It’s scientifically proven.

Your immune system doesn’t improve the most when you experience love, joy, or even deep gratitude — but awe. Awe shifts you on a biochemical level so profoundly that your immune cells have no choice but to perform better.

Standing on a cliff above the sea.
At the shore of the ocean.
Among giant trees.
Watching a sunset.

caption:
Depression, cancer, heart disease, obesity, diabetes, dementia, allergies, asthma, chronic fatigue, autoimmune disease, and more are all inflammatory diseases.

That begs the question, what is causing all this rampant inflammation? It’s mostly our food—too many inflammatory foods and not enough anti-inflammatory foods.

While many foods can trigger inflammation, food is also the most powerful source of anti-inflammatory compounds. Plant-based foods contain over 25,000+ phytochemicals, many of which are potent anti-inflammatories. The polyphenols in colorful plant foods are some of the best inflammation-fighting compounds nature has to offer!

Extra virgin olive oil, for example, contains oleocanthal, which activates the same anti-inflammatory receptors as ibuprofen—without the side effects.

Spices are anti-inflammatory powerhouses too, including:
- Turmeric
- Ginger
- Rosemary

Cooking your meat with spices can neutralize inflammation, while omega-3 fats from wild fish, seafood, and certain nuts and seeds also fight inflammation. Medicinal mushrooms such as shiitake, maitake, reishi, and chaga contain powerful immune-boosting and anti-cancer compounds called polysaccharides.

Nutrient-dense foods rich in vitamin C, zinc, selenium, and vitamin D can further reduce inflammation. 

For example:
- Guavas & parsley (vitamin C)
- Pumpkin seeds & oysters (zinc)
- Brazil nuts & sardines (selenium)
- Porcini mushrooms & herring (vitamin D)

The best thing you can do for your health? Cut out or cut down on inflammatory foods and fill your plate with anti-inflammatory ones!
